entries.text: The 1955 Goldberg is still the shock that made Bach’s variations a public event on the piano. No repeats, about thirty-eight minutes: lines cut with a clarity that was almost theatrical for its day. Beside Schiff’s long Decca survey it is another work — a debut document, not a cycle that unfolds. Beside Gould’s own 1981 remake it is the hotter, leaner object. Gould later disliked some of its tempi and the nocturnal Variation 25; that regret does not retire the disc. For a first piano Goldberg in the house, this remains the Référence: the performance that opened the door.

entries.text: Gould’s 1981 remake is a late architecture — selected first-half repeats, about fifty-one minutes — built around canons and four-part writing rather than debut bravura. Beside the 1955 Référence it is the deeper second thought; beside Schiff’s Decca it remains Gould’s instrument and Gould’s edit, not a complete-repeats survey. Keep both Goulds if you can. If the shelf has room for only one late-studio piano Goldberg, this is the disc — without displacing 1955 as the landmark.

entries.text: Schiff’s first studio Goldberg restores the duration and symmetry the mono debut refused. Near-complete repeats, about seventy-two minutes, thought in three large arcs; some repeats taken an octave up or down, a habit he later dropped. Against Gould 1955 it is another pianist’s complete-repeats world; against Gould 1981 it is warmer and less canonic in obsession. A serious piano alternative on the shelf, not a third Gould. Do not confuse it with the ECM Basel live remake of 2001.
